item.title: Map Apps Are All Handling ‘Lake America’ Differently
item.description:
Three map apps, three responses so far to President Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid an escalating trade war with Canada.

Google changed the lake’s name on its Maps application two days after the Aug. 27 executive order was signed, at least for users in the United States. MapQuest publicly refused to make the update, while Apple on Tuesday began to adopt the new name.

And the tech companies’ decisions seem to matter to Mr. Trump. He had reached out to Apple to ask it to make the change, according to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

“I know that the president reached out to Apple directly,” Mr. Burgum told Fox News on Monday.

Mr. Burgum also said that when place names are ordered to be changed, staff at the Board of Geographic Names “plug that into the software, and then that software cascades down, so all the map providers would do that.”

Noting that the name Lake Ontario is 400 years old, Prime Minister Mark J. Carney of Canada said on social media, “Naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

As of Tuesday evening, the Apple Maps app displayed it as Lake America. It also shows the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America: Mr. Trump ordered that change just after he was inaugurated in January 2025. Google and Apple made the change on their map apps within a month. MapQuest continues to display the Gulf of Mexico.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Google said in a statement: “We update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources.” American users will see Lake America; users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario; and others will see both names displayed, the company said.

The dispute provided an unexpected boost to MapQuest, a pioneering site from the ’90s that had fallen largely into disuse as Google and Apple boomed. It put up a four-word social media post, “We’re not changing it” along with a map labeled “Lake Ontario.”

MapQuest was downloaded 80,000 times on Apple’s iOS platform on Sunday, Forbes reported, citing Appfigures, a market intelligence company. In early August, that figure was around 500 daily downloads on average.

“One basic problem for the mapping companies is that there is no single uncontested authority to defer to,” said David R. Rain, a professor of geography at George Washington University. Map companies must make their own decisions when there is a conflict.

Showing different names to different users depending on their location “may seem like an elegant technical solution,” he said. “But it raises a big huge cartographic question. Is a map telling us what a government calls a place, or what the people who live there call it?”

Noting the increase in downloads for MapQuest after it took a stand against Lake America, Derek H. Alderman, a professor of geography at the University of Tennessee, said that many people wanted map companies to “take a moral stand” on the matter. It matters to them, he said, adding, “Maps and their name places help define the world we come to live in and know.”

“Although map tech companies appear on the surface to be simply about delivering the latest and most accurate geographic information, they are actually deeply involved in the politics of representing the earth and shaping whose histories and identities are given visibility and legitimacy on maps. This is the true pressure and responsibility under which map tech companies work.”

item.title: U.S. Launches Intense New Wave of Attacks in Iran
item.description:
The United States carried out a new wave of attacks against Iran on Tuesday, the latest surge of violence to puncture weeks of relative calm as President Trump has tried to pivot from a military campaign to one of strangling Iran’s economy.

U.S. Central Command said it had struck military targets in Iran in retaliation for attacks on ships and American forces in the region. Hours later, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps said in statements that it had launched missiles on an American military base in Jordan and U.S. military equipment warehouses in Iraq. It warned of fierce retaliations on U.S. interests in the region.

The new strikes came three days after the United States and Iran traded fire for the first time in a month. The latest strikes were far broader and more intense, according to initial reports, and Iranian officials said civilians had been killed, including at a wedding. While it was unclear if the violence would escalate further, the hostilities underscored how remote a durable solution to the conflict remains, six months into a conflict that Mr. Trump once predicted would last a few weeks.

Mr. Trump, in a social media post referring to the Strait of Hormuz, said the U.S. attacks were “large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait.” He added that “if the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level.”

U.S. Central Command said in a statement that it had struck air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities and communications sites.

Iranian state media said projectiles had hit sites in Chabahar and Konarak, southern port cities east of the Strait of Hormuz. Two Iranian officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the U.S. attacks, said the strikes had also hit several other sites across Iran’s southern shores, including a military base in Bandar Abbas, the perimeter of the commercial airport on Qeshm Island and targets in the cities of Sirik and Jask. The officials said the attacks had caused significant damage.

The deputy governor of Hormozgan Province, Ahmad Nafisi, told Iranian state television that a wedding ceremony and a home had been struck in the city of Kuhestak. The Iranian Red Crescent Society, a humanitarian group, reported that four people had been killed, including a child, and 53 others had been injured.

U.S. Central Command said it was aware of the reports. “The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” it said, referring to the Revolutionary Guards.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, said in a social media post that “Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness.” He also put the combined number of those killed and wounded at more than 50.

Photos from Sirik, verified by The New York Times, showed significant damage to a communications tower. Iran’s national electricity company, Tavanir, reported a power outage in some areas of Hormozgan Province because of the airstrikes.

An additional strike hit a residential area around 150 yards from the communications tower. Videos and photographs of the immediate aftermath verified by The Times showed blown- out walls and the collapsed roof and rebar of a smoldering building.

Amid Iran’s statements that it had retaliated against U.S. forces in the region, Jordan said it had been targeted by Iranian missiles, and Kuwait said it had come under an Iranian drone attack.

National security analysts said the latest strikes show how difficult it could be to wind down the conflict.

“I see no fundamental move that either side is now prepared to take that would alter the trajectory and create a pathway out of this,” said Aaron David Miller, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Mr. Miller, who worked for a half-dozen secretaries of states across Democratic and Republican administrations, described the conflict as “wash, rinse and repeat.”

One thing has become clearer, Mr. Miller said: The Iranians are willing to suffer pain, even if to keep Mr. Trump “in the box he created for himself.”

Michael Froman, the president of the Council on Foreign Relations, said a continuing “tit for tat” is most likely for a significant period of time.

“This is probably the new normal for us,” he said of periodic strikes by the U.S., firing on ships and various blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. He added that it was unlikely that there would be a “black and white situation in which there’s a total cease-fire or the Strait of Hormuz is totally open.”

While it has become evident that Mr. Trump wants out of the conflict, Jon Hoffman, a research fellow in defense and foreign policy at the Cato Institute, said, the president will not do so if it looks as if he has failed to project strength and dominance. And Iran is making it increasingly difficult for him to achieve that.

“The idea that Iran would not capitulate and drop to its feet is, to him, a foreign concept,” Mr. Hoffman said.

Oil prices jumped and were up about 4 percent after the U.S. military said it had retaliated over Iranian strikes on commercial ships. Two ships were attacked within minutes of each other on Monday, according to Marisks, a risk consulting firm.

The U.S. military said on Sunday that its forces had bombarded Iranian troops on Larak Island that were preparing to launch rockets armed with mines into the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping corridor for oil and gas. Such an artillery weapon would be unusual, and it was not possible to confirm the military’s report.

The Iranian foreign ministry said several people had been killed and wounded in the strikes on Sunday, but did not provide specifics.

The Revolutionary Guards Corps said it had retaliated by firing at bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates that host U.S. military personnel. The Jordanian authorities said they had intercepted eight missiles in their airspace, while the Emirati military said it had “responded to” a drone from Iran. There were no reports of damage or casualties.

Even as the fighting had slowed in recent weeks, there had been few signs of resolution to the issues at the heart of the war that Mr. Trump began in late February alongside Israel. A “memorandum of understanding” between Tehran and Washington quickly broke down after it was signed in late June.

Since then, Iran has fired on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, severely curbing the ability of U.S. allies to export oil and gas and gaining significant leverage. Iranian officials have demanded steep and immediate concessions in exchange for reopening the strait, which U.S. officials have rejected.

The Trump administration has sought to squeeze Tehran economically by enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports and increasing sanctions on Tehran. But thoroughly enforcing sanctions is notoriously hard, and Iran’s case would require messy run-ins with allies and powerful rivals capable of retaliation, most notably China.

Rozhin Rezai, Malachy Browne, Christiaan Triebert and Jenny Gross contributed reporting.

item.title: Jerome Smith, Freedom Rider Who Challenged Robert Kennedy, Dies at 87
item.description:
Jerome Smith, who as a young Freedom Rider in 1961 was jailed and beaten for his efforts to desegregate transportation in the South, and who excoriated Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy for not doing enough to protect him and the other riders during that harrowing year, died on Aug. 21 at his home in New Orleans. He was 87.

His daughter Farin Smith said the cause was cancer.

When the first Freedom Riders set forth in early May 1961, Mr. Smith was 21 and had dropped out of Southern University in Baton Rouge, La., to devote himself to the Congress of Racial Equality, the civil rights organization known as CORE.

It had been 15 years since the Supreme Court had ruled that segregated seating on interstate buses was unconstitutional. Yet the Southern states had largely ignored the decision. CORE organized a series of Freedom Rides — beginning with teams of Black and white activists who would travel by bus from Washington to New Orleans — to put the ruling to the test, challenging the federal government to finally enforce it.

Mr. Smith — who was stuck in jail in New Orleans, having been arrested after participating in a lunch-counter sit-in — was unable to join the first ride. That journey ended in bloodshed in Alabama, where the young riders were beaten and one bus was firebombed. Senior CORE organizers urged a halt to the rides, but the activists regrouped, and by the end of the month, participants from all over the country were once again heading into the South.

On May 24, Mr. Smith, finally released from jail, boarded a Greyhound bus in Montgomery, Ala., for a ride to Jackson, Miss., where he was promptly arrested. “Breach of peace” was the charge, a coy workaround to flout the law. Like hundreds of other riders who poured into Mississippi that spring, summer and fall, Mr. Smith and his group were moved to Parchman, the notoriously brutal state penitentiary, where they spent their weeks of incarceration irritating the guards by singing protest songs.

Mr. Smith’s second ride was more perilous. On Nov. 29, he and four other CORE members from New Orleans, including 18-year-old Doratha Smith-Simmons, rode a bus to McComb, Miss., a fiercely segregationist community.

The Justice Department had ordered the removal of Jim Crow signs from McComb’s bus terminal. Although the mayor complied, he declared that “our local people are going to respect the color line whether the signs are there or not,” as the historian Raymond Arsenault recounted in “Freedom Riders: 1961 and the Struggle for Racial Justice” (2006).

When Mr. Smith and his group walked into the bus terminal, they were ambushed, beaten with brass knuckles and sticks, and kicked to the pavement outside.

“I thought we would die that day,” Ms. Smith-Simmons said in an interview. She recalled how Mr. Smith had taught her and the others about techniques of nonviolence, and how, the winter before, he had led them in 24 hours of silent fasting in a schoolyard.

“It taught us confidence and it taught us courage,” she said. “It changed my life.”

Mr. Smith suffered a traumatic brain injury from his beating, and for the rest of his life he was bedeviled by headaches and mood swings. Yet he kept working with CORE, traveling the country to raise funds and going through the rural South to register Black voters.

In May 1963, he was in New York City being treated for his lingering injuries when James Baldwin, the celebrated Black author, invited him to a meeting that Mr. Kennedy, the attorney general, had asked Mr. Baldwin to organize with other civil rights advocates, including the playwright Lorraine Hansberry, the musicians Lena Horne and Harry Belafonte and the actor Rip Torn.

The topic was racial justice in Northern cities. But when Mr. Kennedy began to speak about the Justice Department’s efforts, things took a turn.

Mr. Smith began to weep. He angrily declared that he had seen federal forces do little more than stand around as he and his friends were beaten nearly to death. He said that he thought it was hypocritical for the government to ask for his patriotism in supporting the war in Vietnam when it would not protect him and other Black Americans. He added that he would rather die than raise a gun against the Vietnamese people, but that his pacifism was being put to the test at home: He was, he said, “close to the moment where I’m ready to take up a gun.”

Enraged, Mr. Kennedy turned away, at which point Ms. Hansberry and the others lit into him.

“You’ve got a great many very, very accomplished people in this room, Mr. Attorney General,” she said, as Arthur Schlesinger Jr. reported in “Robert Kennedy and His Times” (1978). “But the only man who should be listened to is that man over there,” meaning Mr. Smith.

The meeting devolved from there. Mr. Kennedy seemed incapable of understanding the passion and frustration of the group, and after three hours, the activists walked out. “They seemed possessed,” Mr. Kennedy later told Mr. Schlesinger.

But, Mr. Schlesinger wrote, Mr. Kennedy “began, I believe, to grasp from the inside the nature of Black anguish.”

Mr. Smith said in a 1988 oral history for the Kim Lacy Rogers Collection at the Amistad Research Center in New Orleans that the meeting was a pivotal moment for everyone in the room.

“I remember sitting here and Robert Kennedy sitting there,” he recalled, “and seeing him tremble from the impact of what that struggle gave to me to bring to him.”

Jerome Smith was born on May 21, 1939, in New Orleans. His father, Walter Smith, was a merchant seaman. His mother, Leona (Juluke) Smith, was a seamstress who also worked as a domestic.

He came by his activism naturally; his parents practiced a resolute defiance of Jim Crow laws in their daily lives. Mr. Smith liked to tell the story of how, after seeing his father move a “whites only” barrier on a streetcar to claim a seat, he did the same while riding alone one day when he was 10.

He said he was scooped up by an older Black woman who berated him for his foolhardiness — but, once she hustled him off at the next stop, she threw her arms around him and cried, “Don’t you ever stop doing that!”

Later in life, he remained a stickler for racial justice, forbidding his children to recite the Pledge of Allegiance in class because, as his daughter Farin recalled him telling her principal, “My kids will not honor the American flag because the American flag does not honor Black children.” Nor did they attend school on the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s birthday, long before it became a federal holiday.

In addition to Farin Smith, Mr. Smith is survived by his daughters Kami and Saidah Smith; his son Jerome Jr.; his brothers, Walter Smith Jr. and Archie Sampier; his companion, Cynthia Thornton; and 11 grandchildren. His sons Juden, Tarik and Taju Smith predeceased him, as did his grandson Tarik Jr. His marriage to Betty Watler ended in divorce.

In 1968, he co-founded Tamborine and Fan, an organization that offered to New Orleans children programs in academics, sports, arts and civic engagement, all infused with the city’s Black cultural and musical traditions. He never retired.

He earned the nickname Big Duck, because children followed him around like ducklings.

“He was a pied piper,” Don Hubbard, a New Orleans community activist and entrepreneur, and a friend of Mr. Smith’s from the CORE days, said in an interview. “Education was always his focus and he never got out of that lane.”

In the oral history, Mr. Smith said, “I think the movement was a prayer, the struggle was a prayer, and the failure of the struggle has been our inability to maintain that prayer.”

But, he added, he now saw the struggle succeeding — “through the children.”

item.title: Officer Charged in Shooting of College Athlete Who Knocked at Wrong Door
item.description:
A Pennsylvania police officer committed voluntary manslaughter when he shot a 22-year-old college student who had tried to enter the wrong house after a night of drinking, prosecutors said on Tuesday.

The officer, Sean Farrell, 58, of the Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Department, could face as much as 20 years in prison in the killing of Glenwood Pysher IV. Mr. Pysher, a collegiate baseball player, was preparing for his senior year at Saint Elizabeth University in Florham Park, N.J.

Kevin Steele, Montgomery County’s district attorney, said that Corporal Farrell came to a house in Upper Pottsgrove around 12:30 a.m. on Aug. 23 after a homeowner called 911 to report a man trying to break in. Body camera footage reviewed by prosecutors showed Corporal Farrell walking up the driveway with his gun drawn and Mr. Pysher standing unarmed on the patio, several feet from the back door, the authorities said.

The officer yelled, “Police, let me see your hands,” then yelled, “Hands up, hands up now, drop to the ground!”

Mr. Pysher raised his hands and began walking toward the officer, who again commanded Mr. Pysher to drop and stop. The officer then fired two shots.

Corporal Farrell could have used less deadly weapons, such as his Taser, Mr. Steele said in a statement.

“The officer was a safe distance from Pysher behind a car, and the victim had his hands in the air and did not possess any type of weapon. Mr. Pysher was not a threat,” Mr. Steele said.

Corporal Farrell did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday, and it was not clear whether he had legal representation.

Before the shooting, Mr. Pysher had been barhopping to celebrate a childhood friend’s 21st birthday, according to accounts from friends and the criminal complaint. About 11 p.m., a parent drove Mr. Pysher and others from a bar to the home of the celebrant, friends said.

About 30 minutes later, Mr. Pysher decided to walk to the home of another friend, less than a mile away. He took a wrong turn and ended up at a stranger’s house.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Haitian Student, Despondent Over Ankle Monitor, Dies in Apparent Suicide
item.description:
He was a gifted student, a standout soccer player and a proud cadet in his high school’s J.R.O.T.C. program.

But, his family says, he grew increasingly despondent and humiliated by the ankle monitor he was forced to wear. Not because he was charged with a crime but because he was a Haitian immigrant whose legal status disappeared.

On Monday morning, he walked into oncoming highway traffic outside Springfield, Ohio, and was struck and killed by a truck. Though it is difficult to identify a single cause behind a suicide, his family says the electronic tracking device led Pierre Damas Bel, 20, to lose hope and take his life.

Mr. Bel did not appear to leave behind an explanation of what led him to the side of I-70 in Clark County. But his father and people who knew him described him as a devoted son who had been thriving and excited about studying neuroscience and building a life in the United States.

“Everything was fine with him before this happened,” his father, Pierre Ronal Bel, said in an interview on Monday. “They put an ankle monitor on him and everything changed.”

The Ohio State Highway Patrol said an investigation was ongoing. The county coroner’s office said it would take several weeks for the cause of death to be released.

Gov. Mike DeWine of Ohio called Mr. Bel’s death “a horrible, horrible tragedy” in a news conference Tuesday.

“I think that you know you’ve heard me talk a lot about what I consider to be a very misguided and wrong policy in regard to mass deporting people from this country,” he said.

The younger Mr. Bel came to the United States in 2024, joining his parents and siblings who had arrived a couple of years earlier. He, his parents and a younger sibling were recipients of Temporary Protected Status, a legal safeguard that permitted roughly 330,000 Haitians to live and work in the United States.

The Trump administration ended T.P.S. for Haitians in July and initiated an aggressive electronic monitoring campaign centered on Springfield, which had become a magnet for Haitians in recent years because jobs were plentiful and the cost of living low. It is home to about 60,000 people, including more than 10,000 Haitians.

Mr. Bel’s father said in a statement shared with The New York Times that his son had been taunted because of the ankle monitor.

“He called me at 8:03 on a video call, I’m not feeling OK mentally because of the bullying, and I told him to come home so we can talk,” the father wrote. Three hours later, the police notified him that his son was dead.

In a recent Instagram post, the younger Mr. Bel wrote that he had not come to the United States “to commit a crime or hurt anyone.”

“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to answer questions about Mr. Bel’s death. But it said in a statement that the agency had fitted him with a monitor in July, intended as an alternative to detention that enables authorities to locate immigrants who fail to comply with orders to report for court hearings or ICE check-ins.

“No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a monitor,” the statement read, noting that such immigrants can self-deport.

Mr. Bel had recently started his first semester at Wright State University in Dayton with a scholarship. He was inducted into the National Honor Society at Springfield High School in November, according to photographs and documents provided to The Times. Mr. Bel was co-captain of the soccer team and a lieutenant in the Marine Corps Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps at the high school.

“My son was a bright, very responsible young man who helped his family and studied really hard,” Mr. Bel said in an interview from the duplex that the family bought in Springfield in late 2024. His son had been looking forward to college, he said. .

Miles Dooley, 18, who played soccer with Mr. Bel their senior year, said it was difficult to speak about his friend in the past tense. They were both in the National Honor Society, and Mr. Bel had won a 5-kilometer race to raise money for a local food bank.

“He was so thrilled when he crossed that finish line,” recalled Mr. Dooley, a freshman at Ohio State University. “We had a lot of language barriers on the soccer team, and he often translated for the other kids who didn’t speak as good English.”

On his Instagram account, Mr. Bel posted letters addressed to an immigration judge from teachers, mentors, the manager of the Texas Roadhouse where he had worked and others in support of his request to have the ankle monitor removed. The names were redacted.

The letters from teachers described him as an asset to the school and the broader Springfield community. He excelled academically and volunteered at local charities, they said.

In a letter recommending Mr. Bel for a Rotary scholarship last year, the service manager at the Texas Roadhouse wrote: “Pierre understands the value of hard work and opportunity. He is truly a living breathing example of service above self.”

Mr. Bel was among hundreds of Haitians in Springfield who have been summoned to an ICE office since losing the protection that allowed them to lawfully live and work in the United States. Most who have reported to the agency have been fitted with an ankle monitor, according to lawyers and volunteers who have driven them to the appointments.

A few weeks ago, Haitian leaders told a Times reporter that a star student and athlete had been fitted with an ankle monitor, perhaps the youngest person from Springfield to get one. They were seeking his consent to be interviewed by the reporter, but Mr. Bel never responded.

“This is one of the most tragic outcomes of the Trump cruel and inhumane attacks on the Haitian community,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, a nonprofit.

Since early last month, ICE agents have been roaming Springfield and carrying out arrests almost daily. Lawyers and Haitian leaders estimate that dozens of Haitians have been detained, including two local pastors.

The intensified enforcement has sown widespread fear in the Haitian community, forcing many to venture outside only for work. Some American volunteers have been driving Haitian children to school and others have been delivering groceries to families.

On Sunday, hundreds of faith leaders, community members and other supporters gathered in Springfield to call on ICE to withdraw from the city. The event was titled “Unshackle Springfield.”

Carl Ruby, a local pastor who is the head of an interfaith coalition advocating for Haitians, called on Republican lawmakers to press the Trump administration to change course after Mr. Bel’s death.

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for a list of additional resources.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Shooting at Tucson Gay Bar That Killed 2 Investigated as Hate Crime
item.description:
Two men were killed outside a gay bar in Tucson, Ariz., early Monday morning in a shooting that the police are investigating as a possible hate crime.

A gunman confronted and then shot the two victims in the parking lot of Venture-N, a bar in midtown Tucson, the police said. The authorities identified the two people killed as Vincent Anthony Siqueiros, 42, and Cameron Davis Capara, 33, who were pronounced dead at the scene.

The suspect, identified as Ousman Ceesay, 44, also had gunshot wounds when the police arrived at the bar around 12:30 a.m. on Monday, the authorities said, adding that he died shortly after arriving at a nearby hospital. It was not immediately clear if his wounds were self-inflicted.

Mr. Ceesay was in possession of a note that listed several L.G.B.T.Q.-associated businesses that he may have been targeting, the police said. After the shooting, they increased patrols around L.G.B.T.Q. venues across the city, they said.

He had an address in Oklahoma City, according to public records, and had no criminal history beyond a speeding ticket in 2012. In 2018, he and his then-wife filed for bankruptcy, court records show. Attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. The petition stated that Mr. Ceesay was briefly employed as an Uber and Lyft driver.

Mayor Regina Romero of Tucson called Monday’s shooting a “direct and devastating attack on our L.G.B.T.Q. community” in a video statement she posted on social media. “This tragedy is another painful reminder that homophobia is still rampant in our country,” she added.

Monica Prieto, chief of the Tucson Police Department, said in a statement that “bias-based crimes are especially heinous and have no place in our community.”

The second-largest city in the state, Tucson has long been a progressive pocket in southeast Arizona and has become known for L.G.B.T.Q. activism. After a young gay man, Richard Heakin, was brutally murdered outside a gay bar in 1976, the community rallied and formed Tucson Pride, which worked toward what became some of the first anti-discrimination legislation in the state.

Since then, the Human Rights Campaign has awarded Tucson a score of 100 out of 100 on its municipal equality index, which measures how inclusive a city’s laws, policies and services are. And several L.G.B.T.Q. community organizations have long histories in the area.

Residents described Venture-N as a low-key gathering spot where everyone knew everyone. People come by after work to play pool, sit on the patio to drink beer and catch up with friends, said Sam Cloud, who was appointed to the city’s commission on L.G.B.T.Q. issues.

“It’s been a safe, familiar queer space where people could walk in and feel like they belonged, which is partly of why this hits so hard,” Ms. Cloud said.

The shooting appeared to be an isolated incident, and because the only known suspect died, charges were unlikely to be brought, said Laura Conover, the Pima County attorney.

Reached by phone, Amanda Kate Marquez, 45, Mr. Siqueiros’s sister, said her family was in a state of shock. She described her younger brother as the “funniest, sweetest, most loving human we have ever known.”

Mr. Siqueiros was one of four children and had worked as a restaurant server, Ms. Marquez said. She added that he had made friends wherever he went and was beloved by his nieces and nephews.

“There’s a gigantic gap in all of our hearts that can never be filled,” she said.

Berni Capara, the mother of Mr. Capara, the other victim, described her son as a “wonderful and caring person” who “never judged anyone.” She said that his greatest passion was photography and that he frequently captured images of pro-Palestinian protests and rallies against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement crackdown.

“That somebody would kill him for being gay is just outrageous,” she said.

On Tuesday afternoon outside the bar, a nondescript gray building near downtown Tucson and about a half-mile west of the campus of the University of Arizona, several candles and bouquets of flowers were placed next to photographs of the two victims.

John Cuccini, a regular at the bar, said he had been at Venture-N on Sunday. “It could have been me,” he said. “It could have been any of us.”

Haley Mariscal, a friend of Mr. Capara, drove to Venture-N on Tuesday with her mother, Elizabeth Mariscal, to leave three flower bouquets and two stuffed cats. The elder Ms. Mariscal said they came to show others that both Mr. Capara and Mr. Siqueiros were loved.

Haley Mariscal wept recalling memories of her friend. “He could put a smile on your face if you were having a bad day,” she said of Mr. Capara, adding that he loved his photography work.

“He was so happy,” she said.

Susan C. Beachycontributed research.

item.title: Former President Joe Biden Will Attend Sept. 11 Ceremony in New York
item.description:
Joseph R. Biden Jr. will attend the New York ceremony on Sept. 11 commemorating the 25th anniversary of the most lethal terrorist attacks in U.S. history, filling out the group of former presidents to attend the event.

Mr. Biden and Jill Biden, the former first lady, will be at the event at the World Trade Center site, the former president’s spokesman, T.J. Ducklo, confirmed on Tuesday. A spokeswoman for the National September 11 Memorial and Museum declined to comment.

That sets Mr. Biden apart from his successor. White House officials had initially been preparing for President Trump to be in New York City, his hometown, that day to honor the roughly 3,000 people who were killed when two hijacked commercial planes slammed into the twin towers.

But Mr. Trump decided to skip the ceremony in Lower Manhattan, in part because speeches are not permitted at the event, according to multiple people with knowledge of the discussions. The anniversary of the attacks falls in between a Republican midterm convention that the president and his aides are throwing in Texas, and a golf tournament at the president’s club in Doonbeg, Ireland.

One person briefed on the matter said that traveling overseas is easier if Mr. Trump departs from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than from a commercial airport in New York or New Jersey.

Mr. Trump has also faced threats from Iran amid the war he and Israel began against the country earlier this year, and it was unclear whether security concerns might have factored into the decision.

Though the National September 11 Memorial and Museum had allowed politicians to recite poems and significant American texts, like the Gettysburg Address, the museum since 2012 has prohibited politicians from making remarks. Mr. Trump is expected to instead appear at the Pentagon, which was also struck by a hijacked jetliner on Sept. 11, 2001. The president delivered an address there on Sept. 11 last year.

The New York Times first reported that Mr. Trump would skip the New York ceremony. The White House did not challenge the article when approached for comment. A day later, on Aug. 28, Mr. Trump and his communications director in social media posts claimed the reporting was false. “I would love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members,” Mr. Trump wrote.

Mr. Biden and Dr. Biden will join the three other living former presidents at the New York event. Former President George W. Bush and Laura Bush, the former first lady, are expected to attend; Mr. Bush was about eight months into his first term when the terrorist attacks took place.

Former President Barack Obama, former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton are also expected to attend the ceremony, during which family members of those killed in the attacks will recite the names of the dead, over the course of hours. Mrs. Clinton was a senator from New York when the attacks took place.

item.title: A Nearly 200-Year-Old Museum Known for Its T. Rex Faces Extinction
item.description:
When the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia first opened the doors of its museum, John Quincy Adams was president.

Twenty-four states had been admitted to the union.

And the first skeletal remains of a Tyrannosaurus rex were decades away from being discovered.

But just two years shy of its bicentennial, the venerated museum, which has been affiliated with Drexel University since 2011, is going the way of the dinosaurs.

At the end of September, the facility known for its Dinosaur Hall and its extensive collection of fossils and other specimens will permanently close, a casualty of struggling attendance and rising costs, the academy and the university said in a joint message on Tuesday.

The message was signed by Antonio Merlo, Drexel’s president, and Suzanne Biemiller, chairwoman of the academy’s board, who wrote that the museum had achieved mixed results in trying to rebuild attendance after the Covid-19 pandemic.

“Over time, it became clear that these were not temporary pressures, but fundamental changes in the economics of the academy’s operational model, costs that have imperiled the academy’s ability to discharge its overall mission and preserve its legacy,” they wrote.

The message noted that the academy, which was started in 1812 by seven naturalists, would continue to operate and “to identify new and financially sustainable opportunities for the public display of elements from its collections and engagement with the natural sciences.” On its website, the museum described itself as the “oldest natural history museum in the Americas.”

Drexel, a private institution, has grappled with declining enrollment and budget deficits in the millions. During the past decade, the total number of students has fallen by nearly 21 percent, according to the university, which The Philadelphia Inquirer reported in April had been facing a $20 million budget deficit.

At the same time, the university contributed nearly $17 million total to the academy during the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years, according to audited financial statements on the university’s website. The academy also had a $5 million line of credit from the university, from which it had drawn $2.4 million as of June 30, 2025, those records showed.

The difficulties experienced by the academy, which is a nonprofit subsidiary of the university, also reflect the pain that is being felt by many museums in the current political and economic climate.

At more than half of museums in the United States, attendance totals have not returned to prepandemic levels, according to a 2025 survey by the American Alliance of Museums. That erosion has overlapped with economic uncertainty and a pressure campaign on museums by the Trump administration, which has tied federal funding and tax-exempt status to the rejection of diversity initiatives and exhibits it perceives as un-American.

Last year, the museum scaled back its hours of operation.

In response to questions on Tuesday from The New York Times, a Drexel University spokesman, Britt Faulstick, said that 27 of the academy’s 80 employees would be affected by the museum’s closure. He did not elaborate on their employment status.

As Philadelphians began to grasp a future without the museum, people in the community lamented the closure. Some recounted sleepovers among the exhibits with scouting and other youth groups, including the Camp Fire girls. Others wondered what would happen to its life-size dinosaur replicas, including a cast of a Tyrannosaurus rex.

“This is crazy and needs to be rectified,” Daniel Pearson, an editorial writer and columnist for The Inquirer, wrote on social media on Tuesday. “It is genuinely hard to believe that the city cannot sustain a museum that’s been around since before the Civil War.”

Asked about the museum’s dinosaur collection, Mr. Faulstick said he could not confirm any specific plans while noting that the university and the academy were “identifying new opportunities to ensure access to its collections and public engagement in the natural sciences.”

The offices of Mayor Cherelle Parker of Philadelphia and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday about the museum’s plans to close.

]]>
